newsitem.title: USA: Coastal founder Oscar Wyatt to step down.
newsitem.headline: Coastal founder Oscar Wyatt to step down.

text.p: Coastal Corp. said Tuesday founder and Chairman Oscar Wyatt, one of the oil industry's most flamboyant figures, would step down in July.
Wyatt told Reuters in an interview it was time to make room for younger executives, but that he expected his successors to maintain the firm's tradition as an aggressive maverick.
"I'll be 73 years old on July 11. It's not enough, but I think it's time we let the young'uns fight," he said.
Wyatt said his departure was not linked to an oil trading scandal at the company that recent news reports said had drawn the attention of the FBI.

Coastal said it fired three traders in February who were suspected of siphoning off oil trading profits. Wyatt said federal investigators would likely find similar problems at other companies and that the financial impact on Coastal was "negligible."

Coastal said current President and Chief Executive Officer David Arledge will take over as chairman when Wyatt leaves on July 15. Wyatt said Arledge would continue Coastal's tradition as "a rolling up the sleeves and getting in the scrap company... I don't think we'll lose any of our aggressiveness."
Wyatt pledged to remain active in the company as a member of its board of directors.

Wyatt built Coastal into an energy giant from humble beginnings. In 1951, using $800 he got on a loan against his car, he and a partner started the Hardly Able Oil Co. From that tiny firm, Wyatt, in 1955, formed Coastal States Oil and Gas Co., which eventually became today's $11 billion Coastal Corp.

Along the way, the gruff, headstrong Wyatt became an influential figure in the world oil industry, with close contacts in the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries and high-level political connections around the world. But he also invited controversy by sometimes working at the margins of U.S. foreign policy in the search for new sources of oil and new markets.
Under Wyatt, Coastal struck deals in the 1980s with Iraq and libya, the latter of which drew a censure from the U.S. government.

In December 1990, just before the outbreak of the Gulf War, Wyatt and fellow Coastal board member John Connally went to Baghdad to meet with Saddam Hussein, where they secured the release of 32 U.S. hostages.
Wyatt said he was always motivated by a global vision of the oil industry that sometimes conflicted with official policy. "We're buying Iraqi oil today and a lot of people think that's a sin."
But he said he opposed "any unilateral action of any type by the United States" such as oil embargos because they accomplished little and put U.S. firms at a disadvantage.
His conflicts were not always overseas. In the mid-1970s, Coastal angered many Texas customers, including utilities and cities, when it was unable to deliver natural gas at agreed-upon prices.
A huge legal controversy was finally settled when Coastal agreed to split off part of its natural gas operations into what is now Valero Energy Corp. in San Antonio, Texas.
